igloo.e: From Inuktitut ᐃᒡᓗ (iclo, “house, building (of any kind)”), from Proto-Inuit *əɣlu, from Proto-Eskimo *əŋlu.

s.d: an Eskimo hut; usually built of blocks (of sod or snow) in the shape of a dome
A dome-shaped Inuit shelter, constructed of blocks cut from snow.
A cavity, or excavation, made in the snow by a seal, over its breathing hole in the sea ice.
A reinforced bunker for the storage of nuclear weapons.
x: General James Walsh signalled Strategic Air Command that the B-47 tore apart the igloo and knocked about 3 mark sixes.

s.d: A kind of airfreight cargo container.
x: Since most major airlines have interline agreements, if your cargo is in an igloo or container, it can be moved as is […]

s.d: an Eskimo hut; usually built of blocks (of sod or snow) in the shape of a dome

igneous.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁engʷ-
Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnís
Proto-Italic *engʷnis
Latin ign(is)
Proto-Indo-European *-éyos
Proto-Italic *-ejos
Proto-Italic *-eos
Latin -eus
Latin igneusbor.
English igneous
From Latin igneus (“fiery”). By surface analysis, Latin ign- + -eous.

s.d: produced under conditions involving intense heat
x: igneous rock is rock formed by solidification from a molten state; especially from molten magma
igneous fusion is fusion by heat alone

s.d: produced by the action of fire or intense heat
x: rocks formed by igneous agents

s.d: like or suggestive of fire
x: a fiery desert wind
an igneous desert atmosphere

s.d: Pertaining to or having the nature of fire; containing fire; resembling fire.
x: The stone had an igneous appearance.

s.d: Resulting from, or produced by, great heat. With rocks, it could also mean formed from lava or magma.
x: Granite and basalt are igneous rocks.
All formations, whether igneous or aqueous, which can be shown by any such proofs to be of a date posterior to the introduction of man, will be called Recent.

s.d: rock formed by the solidification of molten magma
(uncountable) One of the major groups of rock that makes up the crust of the Earth; formed by the cooling of molten rock, either below the surface (intrusive) or on the surface (extrusive).

ignescent.e: Latin ignescens, present participle of ignescere (“to become inflamed”), from ignis (“fire”): compare French ignescent. By surface analysis, Latin ign- + -escent.

s.d: A stone that emits sparks of fire when struck with steel.
can emit sparks or burst into flame
Emitting sparks of fire when struck with steel; scintillating.
x: ignescent stones

ignis fatuus.e: From New Latin ignis fatuus (literally “foolish fire”).

s.d: a pale light sometimes seen at night over marshy ground
an illusion that misleads
A will o' the wisp.
x: Fiery spirits or devils are such as commonly work by blazing stars, fire-drakes, or ignes fatui; which lead men often in flumina aut præcipitia, saith Bodine[…]
An Ignis Fatuus, that bewitches, / And leads Men into Pools and Ditches

s.d: (figuratively) A delusion, a false hope.
x: […] they think this is written on purpose to be published; and that this defence is so published, that it may serve as an Ignis fatuus to mislead them […]
He cursed the journey he had been led to take after what had proved but an ignis fatuus, deluded as he had been by false expectations;[…]

ignite.e: From Latin ignītus, past participle of igniō, ignire (“to set on fire, ignite”), from Latin ignis (“fire”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis, and thus related to Sanskrit अग्नि (agní), Lithuanian ugnis, and Russian ого́нь (ogónʹ).

s.d: cause to start burning; subject to fire or great heat
x: Great heat can ignite almost any dry matter
Light a cigarette

s.d: start to burn or burst into flames
x: Marsh gases ignited suddenly
The oily rags combusted spontaneously

s.d: arouse or excite feelings and passions
x: The ostentatious way of living of the rich ignites the hatred of the poor
The refugees' fate stirred up compassion around the world

s.d: start or maintain a fire in
x: fire the furnace

s.d: To set fire to (something), to light (something)
To spark off (something), to trigger
x: ignite curiosity
ignite someone's interest

s.d: To commence burning.
To subject to the action of intense heat; to heat strongly; often said of incombustible or infusible substances.
x: to ignite iron or platinum

s.d: set afire
x: the ignited paper
a kindled fire

s.d: a substance used to ignite or kindle a fire
a device for lighting or igniting fuel or charges or fires
x: do you have a light?

s.d: Any device that is used to ignite something, especially a fuel mixture, or a charge of explosive
capable of burning
Capable of being ignited.

the mechanism that ignites the fuel in an internal-combustion engine
the act of setting something on fire
(uncountable) The act of igniting.
(uncountable) The initiation of combustion.
(uncountable) A system for activating combustion in a combustion engine.
(uncountable) Receptacle for a key used to start the engine in a vehicle.
x: Put the key in the ignition and turn it right.

an induction coil that converts current from a battery into the high-voltage current required by spark plugs

a device that prevents an automotive engine from starting

a key that operates the ignition switch of an automotive engine
A key that starts the combustion engine of a motor vehicle.
x: She fitted the ignition-key into the switch deftly.

s.d: a restraint incorporated into the ignition switch to prevent the use of a vehicle by persons who do not have the key
switch that operates a solenoid that closes a circuit to operate the starter
the mechanism that ignites the fuel in an internal-combustion engine
a substance used to ignite or kindle a fire
a device for lighting or igniting fuel or charges or fires
x: do you have a light?

ignobility.e:
From Latin ignōbilitās.
By surface analysis, ignoble + -ity.

s.d: the quality of being ignoble
(uncountable) The state or condition of being ignoble.

ignoble.e: Borrowed from Middle French ignoble, from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).

s.d: To make ignoble; to bring low.
completely lacking nobility in character or quality or purpose
x: something cowardly and ignoble in his attitude
I think it a less evil that some criminals should escape than that the government should play an ignoble part

s.d: not of the nobility
x: of ignoble (or ungentle) birth
untitled civilians

s.d: Not noble; plebeian; common.
x: I was not ignoble of descent.

s.d: Not honorable; base.
x: A base, ignoble mind, / That mounts no higher than a bird can soar.
far from the madding crowd's ignoble strife

s.d: Not a true or "noble" falcon; said of certain hawks, such as the goshawk.
Of an element, dangerously reactive.
the quality of being ignoble
(uncountable) Synonym of ignobility

ignobly.e:
Etymology tree
English ignoble
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English ignobly
From ignoble + -ly.

s.d: in a currish manner; meanspiritedly
x: he behaved ignobly

s.d: in an ignoble manner
x:
No villanous bounty yet hath past my heart;
Vnwisely, not ignobly haue I giuen.
Deep would have been the blot upon his escutcheon if his chocolate had been ignobly waited on by only three men; he must have died of two.

ignominious.e: From Late Middle English ignominious (“disgraceful, shameful”), from Middle French ignominieux (modern French ignominieux), or from its etymon Latin ignōminiōsus (“disgraced; disgraceful, shameful, ignominious”), from ignōminia (“disgrace, dishonour, shame, ignominy”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overly; prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Ignōminia is derived from ig- (variant of in- (prefix meaning not) + nōmen (“name; good name, reputation”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁

s.d: (used of conduct or character) deserving or bringing disgrace or shame
x: Man … has written one of his blackest records as a destroyer on the oceanic islands
an ignominious retreat

s.d: Especially of a person: deserving of disgrace or dishonour; contemptible, despicable.
Causing or marked by disgrace or dishonour; disgraceful, dishonourable; also (loosely), humiliating, shameful.
x: The time when the pseudovirtuous men and women die a painful and ignominious death has yet to come.
Hath he not tvvit our Soueraigne Lady here / VVith ignominious vvords, though Clarkely coucht? / As if ſhe had ſuborned ſome to ſvveare / Falſe allegations, to o'rethrovv his ſtate.

ignominiously.e:
Etymology tree
English ignominious
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English ignominiously
From ignominious + -ly (suffix forming adverbs from nouns). Ignominious is derived from Late Middle English ignominious (“disgraceful, shameful”), from Middle French ignominieux (modern French ignominieux), or from its etymon Latin ignōminiōsus (“disgraced; disgraceful, shameful, ignominious”), from ignōminia (“disgrace, dishonour, shame, ignominy”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overly; prone to’ forming

s.d: in a dishonorable manner or to a dishonorable degree
x: his grades were disgracefully low

s.d: In a manner which is ignominious (“especially of a person: deserving of disgrace or dishonour; contemptible, despicable; (generally) causing or marked by disgrace or dishonour; disgraceful, dishonourable; also (loosely), humiliating, shameful”).
x: Men ignorant in letters, ſtudious for their bellies, and ignominiouſly lazie, vnleſſe ſome fevv that giue themſelues to nauigation; and become indifferent good Pilots.
But the death of the royal captive, vvho vvas ignominiouſly beheaded, diſgraced the triumph of Rome and of Chriſtianity; […]

s.d: unworthiness meriting public disgrace and dishonor
(uncountable) The state or quality of being ignominious.

ignominy.e: Borrowed from French ignominie, from Latin ignōminia, from ig- (“not”) + nomen (“name”) (prefix assimilated form of in-).

s.d: a state of dishonor
x: one mistake brought shame to all his family
suffered the ignominy of being sent to prison

s.d: (uncountable) Great dishonor, shame, or humiliation.
x: Near-synonym: bad name
But like Czar Peter content to toil in the shipyards of foreign cities, Queequeg disdained no seeming ignominy, if thereby he might happily gain the power of enlightening his untutored countrymen.

ignoramus.e: After the ignorant lawyer Ignoramus, the titular character in the 1615 play Ignoramus by the English playwright George Ruggle; from Latin ignōrāmus (“we do not know, we are unacquainted with, we are ignorant of”), the first-person plural present active indicative of ignōrō (“to not know, to be unacquainted with, to be ignorant of”).

s.d: an ignorant person
A totally ignorant person—unknowledgeable, uneducated, or uninformed; a fool.
x: The problem is that visual ignoramuses, such as this writer, can't think of that many pictures and end up drawing question marks where a frog should be.
“The cost of appearing with this bloviating ignoramus is obvious, it seems to me,” he said on “This Week,” the ABC News program.

s.d: (dated) A grand jury's ruling on an indictment when the evidence is determined to be insufficient to send the case to trial.
To make such a ruling against (an indictment).

ignorance.e:
From Middle English ignoraunce, ignorance, from
From Old French ignorance, from Latin ignōrantia. By surface analysis, ignor(e) + -ance.

s.d: the lack of knowledge or education
(uncountable) The condition of being uninformed or uneducated; lack of knowledge or information.
x: She shows total ignorance about the topic at hand.
There had been the whisky and Perrier in the morning but, in my ignorance of alcoholics then, I could not imagine one whisky harming anyone who was driving in an open car in the rain.

s.d: (uncountable) Sins committed through ignorance.
(uncountable) Existential blindness.

ignorant.e: From Old French ignorant, from Latin ignōrāns (“unaware, unknowing”). By surface analysis, ignore + -ant.

s.d: One who is ignorant.
uneducated in general; lacking knowledge or sophistication
x: an ignorant man
nescient of contemporary literature

s.d: uneducated in the fundamentals of a given art or branch of learning; lacking knowledge of a specific field
x: she is ignorant of quantum mechanics
he is musically illiterate

s.d: unaware because of a lack of relevant information or knowledge
x: he was completely ignorant of the circumstances
an unknowledgeable assistant

s.d: Unknowledgeable or uneducated; characterized by ignorance.
x: That man that doth not know those things which are of use and necessity for him to know, is but an ignorant man, whatever he may know besides;
The ignorant peasant, without fault, is greater than the philosopher with many; for what is genius or courage without an heart?

s.d: Not knowing (a fact or facts), unaware (of something).
x: For we would not, brethren, have you ignorant of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life:

Eve. Somewhat forbids me, which I cannot name;
For ignorant of guilt, I fear not shame:
But some restraining thought, I know not why,
Tells me, you long should beg, I long deny.

s.d: (slang) Ill-mannered, crude.
x: His manner was at best off-hand, at worst totally ignorant.

s.d: (obsolete) Unknown; undiscovered
x: Alas, what ignorant sin have I committed?

[…] I beseech you,
If you know aught which does behove my knowledge
Thereof to be inform’d, imprison't not
In ignorant concealment.

s.d: Resulting from ignorance; foolish; silly.
x:
[…] his shipping—
Poor ignorant baubles!— upon our terrible seas,
Like eggshells moved upon their surges, crack’d
As easily ’gainst our rocks:

ignorance (especially of orthodox beliefs)

ignoratio elenchi.e: From Latin ignōrātiō elenchī (“ignorance of the refutation”).

s.d: the logical fallacy of supposing that an argument proving an irrelevant point has proved the point at issue
(uncountable) The fallacy of presenting an argument that may or may not be logically valid, but fails to address the issue in question.

English ignore
From French ignorer, from Latin ignōrō (“to have no knowledge of, mistake, take no notice of, ignore”), from ignārus (“not knowing”), from in- (“not”) + gnārus (“knowing”), from gnōscō, nōscō; see know.

s.d: refuse to acknowledge
x: She cut him dead at the meeting

s.d: bar from attention or consideration
x: She dismissed his advances

s.d: fail to notice
give little or no attention to
x: Disregard the errors

s.d: To deliberately not listen or pay attention to.
x: A problem ignored is a problem doubled.
Ignore these four words.

s.d: To pretend to not notice someone or something.
(obsolete) Not to know.
disregarded
x: his cries were unheeded
Shaw's neglected one-act comedy, ‘A Village Wooing’

iguana.e: Borrowed from Spanish iguana, from Taíno *iwana.

s.d: large herbivorous tropical American arboreal lizards with a spiny crest along the back; used as human food in Central America and South America
A green iguana (Iguana iguana), a large tropical American lizard often kept as a pet.
x: The problem with keeping the green iguana as a pet is that they are often misfed. For example, some will feed them meat or meat-based foods […]

s.d: Any member of the genus Iguana.
(colloquial) In America and the Pacific, any of several members of the lizard family Iguanidae.
x: Marine iguanas line the shores of the islands, and are usually seen sprawled over lava rocks near the sea.

s.d: (colloquial) In Africa, any large member of the genus Varanus, especially the aquatic Nile monitor (see leguan).
(Australia) Any member of the genus Varanus (see goanna).
x: The last they had had, was an iguana one of the blacks had brought in; and though he felt disgusted at the idea of eating it, he made up into a kind of stew, and they both enjoyed it immensely.

s.d: lizards of the New World and Madagascar and some Pacific islands; typically having a long tail and bright throat patch in males
Any lizard of the family Iguanidae.
lizards of the New World and Madagascar and some Pacific islands; typically having a long tail and bright throat patch in males

iguanodon.e: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Iguanodon, from Spanish iguana (from Taíno *iwana) + translingual -odon.

s.d: massive herbivorous bipedal dinosaur with a long heavy tail; common in Europe and northern Africa; early Cretaceous period
Any large dinosaur of the genus †Iguanodon, of the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.
x: August the twenty-eighth - the day we saw five live iguanodons in a glade of Maple White Land.
